title: Quantized Contract Autoscaler with Surge Fences and Conservative Fallbacks
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Purpose: Implement an autoscaling policy engine that enforces contractual throughput guarantees (per-tenant and per-fleet), prioritizes latency SLOs, and prevents unsafe surge behavior via 'surge fences' (rate/ramp limits, absolute caps). This ticket defines the policy, scaling algorithm composition, safety limits, config surface, telemetry, and rollout plan for the Quantized Contract Autoscaler (QCA).

Motivation and context:
- Customers on Dedicated buy throughput commitments (e.g., X tpm, Y concurrent contexts) and expect predictable latency. Autoscalers must satisfy those contracts while keeping cost and reliability constraints.
- Existing controllers either over-react to short bursts or rely on simple thresholds that produce oscillation during transient spikes. We need a multi-stage controller with conservative safety overrides and contract-aware headroom.

Target metrics and objectives:
- Primary objective: maintain p95 token latency <= configured SLA per-contract tier (e.g., 150ms for tier-1).
- Secondary objective: meet committed throughput (effective tokens/sec or requests/sec) against contract-level windows (1m, 5m, 1h).
- Cost objective: avoid unnecessary instance spin-ups; prefer batching and KV-cache hotspots before scaling.
- Safety objective: avoid scaling actions that exceed per-fleet budget caps, ramp-rate limits, or violate global capacity constraints.

Metric inputs (signals):
- Observed throughput (req/s and tokens/s) per tenant and aggregated at fleet level (1s, 30s, 5m windows).
- Latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) for token generation and end-to-end request.
- Instance utilization (GPU mem, avg token generation time, concurrency slots used).
- KV cache hit ratio and session affinity churn.
- Forecasted demand: short-horizon forecast produced by lightweight EWMA + seasonality detector (fast path) and optional Tensor-based predictor (slow path) for scheduled spikes.

Scaling algorithm composition (multi-stage):
1) Forecast + demand smoothing: produce a smoothed target throughput for the next 60s using EWMA with configurable half-life; if scheduled event flagged, inject predicted multiplier.
2) PID-like corrective loop: compute error = target_throughput - observed_capacity; PID controller suggests delta instances based on recent errors and derivative to reduce overshoot. PID gains default conservative; can be tuned per-customer class.
3) Budget-aware quantization: convert continuous delta to discrete "contract quanta" (smallest billable capacity unit) and clamp by customer's reserved pool and remaining budget. This enforces that we only provision in increments consistent with pricing and guarantees.
4) Safety fence layer: apply hard constraints before action: min/max node counts, per-minute ramp percent (e.g., max +20%/min), global fleet ceilings, and a per-tenant emergency cap to prevent noisy neighbor blowouts. If action violates any fence, it's suppressed and a fallback policy runs.
5) Conservative fallback: when a scale-up is suppressed, trigger short-term mitigations in priority order: increase batching target, prefer heavier KV cache allocation, throttle low-priority tenants, route excess requests to a lower-cost model variant with knobbed context length.
6) Post-action stabilization: after a scale event, enforce a cooldown window (configurable, default 90s) and monitor for oscillation; if oscillation detected run exponential backoff on future scale-downs.

Safety limits and policies:
- Absolute min_nodes and max_nodes per fleet (configurable per-ring).
- Ramp limits: percent-based per-minute and absolute delta per action.
- Contract credit budget: persistent headroom accounting that prevents using more than N minutes of extra capacity without manual approval.
- Rapid rollback gates: any scale action that causes latency regressions (p95 increase > 20% vs baseline) is automatically reverted and flagged.
- Cross-tenant fairness: fairness arbiter reduces allocations to non-committed tenants if a contracted tenant requires headroom.

Config surface (operator + customer knobs):
- target_metric: [p95_latency | throughput | weighted_mix].
- lookahead_window_seconds: integer.
- quantization_unit: instance_count or throughput_quanta.
- pid_gains: "P", "I", "D" as floats (defaults conservative).
- ramp_pct_per_min, max_delta_per_action, cooldown_seconds.
- emergency_policy: [throttle_noncommitted | route_to_variant | request_rejection].
- enable_predictor: boolean (use slow ML predictor).

Telemetry and observability requirements:
- Emit event for every decision with tags: tenant_id, decision_type (scale_up/scale_down/suppress/fallback), reason_codes (forecast_error, ramp_limit, budget_exceeded), metrics_snapshot, proposed_delta, final_delta.
- Dashboards: per-tenant headroom utilization, suppressed_action_rate, fallback_invocations, scale_latency impact charts.
- SLO alerting: if suppressed_action_rate > 0.5% for >10m for contracted tenants => SEV ticket.

Implementation notes and tradeoffs considered:
- We purposely quantize to contract units to keep billing alignment and avoid tiny oscillatory changes. This makes the controller less agile for microbursts; mitigations rely on batching and KV cache before scale.
- Forecast ML models provide better accuracy for scheduled spikes but are heavier; they are opt-in and produce a separate signal so we degrade gracefully without them.
- PID controller chosen for simplicity and interpretability; a full RL controller was considered but deferred due to safety and explainability requirements.
- Surge fences are intentionally conservative (favoring system stability over immediate SLO compliance in ambiguous cases). In practice we'll tune fences using canaries and A/B experiments.

Testing, rollout and verification:
- Unit tests for decision logic and fence composition.
- Integration tests in staging with synthetic workloads: steady increase, sinusoidal load, bursty Poisson load.
- Canary rollout plan: enable QCA for 5 low-risk customers first (feature flag), monitor suppressed_action_rate, p95 latency, and fallback_invocations for 48h. If metrics stable, expand to 30 customers, then gradually to all contracted tenants.
- Chaos scenarios: simulate node flaps and network partitions to confirm fallback behavior and safe rollbacks.

Docs and operational artifacts to update:
- Console docs: autoscaling policy UI, new knobs, and interpretation guidance.
- Runbook: incident steps for suppressed_action_rate alerts and rollback procedures.
- Telemetry spec in Observability repo (links below).

Links and artifacts:
- Design doc (internal): https://docs.redwood.ai/dedicated/qca-design (placeholder)
- PR draft: https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/1879
- Staging experiment dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/qca-staging (placeholder)

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Default contract quantization size: 1 instance vs 0.2 instance-equivalent throughput quanta. Recommendation: start at 1 instance-equivalent to limit churn.
- How to bill temporary overages consumed via emergency headroom — credit accounting vs automatic invoicing. Needs PM/legal guidance.
- Whether to expose advanced PID tuning fields to customers or keep as operator-managed. Recommendation: operator-managed with tier presets.

Next steps (short-term action items):
- (Assignee) implement decision event schema and basic policy loop skeleton (week 1).
- (SRE) add telemetry counters and suppressed_action_rate alert (week 1).
- (Research) prototype fast EWMA predictor and evaluate accuracy on last 6 months of traffic (week 2).
- (PM) finalize billing semantics for emergency headroom (week 2).

Acceptance criteria:
- QCA can make scaling decisions for a test fleet and emit decision events.
- Telemetry shows suppressed_action_rate, fallback_invocations, and headroom utilization.
- Canary customers observe no >2x p95 regression and suppressed_action_rate <0.5% over 48h.
- Operational runbook and console knobs updated.
